body:
Energy access involves more than producing electricity

Electricity is an essential part of economic infrastructure. It serves households, agriculture, industry and public institutions. However, generating electricity at a power station does not automatically mean that every household can use it. Electricity must also reach consumers through transmission lines, distribution networks and individual connections.

Government energy programmes address different stages of this process. Some extend electricity networks to villages, some provide connections to households, and others support renewable electricity generation or improve the timing of agricultural supply.

Cooking energy forms another part of household energy access. A family may have electricity but still depend on firewood for cooking. Programmes supporting liquefied petroleum gas, or LPG, therefore address a different requirement.

Five distinct forms of government support

Form of supportWhat it providesScheme example
Network developmentElectricity lines, distribution infrastructure and village electrificationDDUGJY
Consumer connectionAn electricity or LPG connection for an eligible householdSaubhagya; PM Ujjwala
Generation assistanceSupport for installing solar electricity systemsPM Surya Ghar; PM-KUSUM
Supply arrangementElectricity made available during specified hoursGujarat Kisan Suryoday
Subsidy deliveryTransfer of an applicable financial benefit to a consumerPAHAL

The same household can benefit from more than one type of support. For example, a family may receive an electricity connection through an electrification programme and later install rooftop solar under a different programme. Receiving a connection does not itself establish eligibility for a solar subsidy.

Which level of government is responsible?

Electricity is a subject in the Concurrent List of the Constitution. Both the Union and the States have legislative roles. In practice, electricity supply and distribution to consumers are primarily handled by State Governments and distribution utilities, commonly called DISCOMs. Union schemes may finance or support these activities without replacing the State's responsibility for supplying electricity.

Different Union ministries administer different types of schemes:

  • Ministry of Power: rural electrification and distribution-network programmes.
  • Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE): rooftop solar and solar agricultural programmes.
  • Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas: LPG connections and LPG subsidy arrangements.

Gujarat also implements its own energy initiatives through the State Government and its power-sector institutions.

Status matters: A scheme may remain important for understanding India's energy policy even after its implementation period has ended. Historical achievements must not be confused with an open application programme. The status descriptions in this lesson use 16 November 2026 as the content cutoff.

Prelims focus

  • DDUGJY concerns rural electricity infrastructure and village electrification.
  • Saubhagya concerns electricity connections to willing unelectrified households.
  • PM Surya Ghar concerns residential rooftop solar.
  • PM-KUSUM concerns solar energy for agriculture.
  • PM Ujjwala provides eligible LPG connections; PAHAL transfers applicable LPG subsidies.
  • Trap: Connection, continuous supply, solar installation and subsidy transfer are different benefits.

[Sources: NCERT, Indian Economic Development, Class 11, Chapter 8, 'Infrastructure', especially Section 8.5, 'Energy'; NCERT, Resources and Development, Class 8, Chapter 3, 'Mineral and Power Resources', section 'Power Resources'; Ministry of Power, 'Electrification of Villages', 12 February 2026, PIB Release 2226925; consulted 16 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Electricity access transforms how a rural household meets its daily energy needs.

title: Energy Programmes: Understanding Their Different Purposes

body:
Purpose and administrative authority

Deen Dayal Upadhyaya Gram Jyoti Yojana (DDUGJY) was introduced by the Government of India in December 2014. It was administered under the Ministry of Power and implemented through State power-sector agencies and distribution utilities.

The scheme addressed the infrastructure needed to supply electricity to rural India. Its intended beneficiaries were rural villages, their households, agricultural consumers and other users dependent on the rural distribution network.

The main components of DDUGJY

  • Village electrification: Extending the electricity network to inhabited villages that had not been electrified.
  • Feeder separation: Separating agricultural electricity feeders from feeders serving non-agricultural consumers, where required.
  • Distribution-system strengthening: Improving infrastructure such as distribution lines, transformers and associated equipment.
  • Metering: Providing meters at appropriate points, including feeders, distribution transformers and consumers.
  • Household connections: Supporting specified rural household-electrification works, including connections for eligible below-poverty-line households.

Why separate agricultural and non-agricultural feeders?

A feeder is an electricity-distribution circuit that carries power from a substation towards consumers. In a village, the electricity requirements of irrigation pumps differ from those of households and public services. Separate agricultural feeders allow the utility to schedule irrigation supply independently of other rural consumers.

Feeder separation is therefore an infrastructure measure. It does not mean that every agricultural consumer automatically receives an individual solar pump, nor does it guarantee any particular daily supply duration under DDUGJY itself.

What did village electrification mean?

Under the Rural Electrification Policy, 2006, a village could be reported as electrified when basic electricity-distribution infrastructure was available in inhabited localities, including hamlets inhabited by weaker sections where present; electricity was provided to public institutions such as schools or panchayat offices; and at least 10% of households had electricity connections.

The 10% figure was a minimum condition for the administrative classification of a village. It was not a target to stop connecting households once 10% had electricity.

An electrified village is not necessarily a fully electrified village. A village could satisfy the official village-electrification definition while many individual households still lacked connections. This distinction explains why household electrification required separate attention.

Completion and current status

According to information reported by States and published by the Ministry of Power on 12 February 2026, all previously unelectrified inhabited census villages were reported electrified by 28 April 2018. The Ministry reported 18,374 villages electrified under DDUGJY.

DDUGJY closed on 31 March 2022. As of 16 November 2026, it is a completed historical scheme, not an ongoing programme for fresh DDUGJY applications. The Revamped Distribution Sector Scheme (RDSS), launched in 2021, is a separate, ongoing Union programme supporting distribution improvements and specified household-electrification works.

Prelims focus

  • Full name: Deen Dayal Upadhyaya Gram Jyoti Yojana.
  • Launch: December 2014; Union Ministry: Ministry of Power.
  • Main components: rural electrification, feeder separation, distribution strengthening and metering.
  • Village-electrification definition: at least 10% household connections, together with infrastructure and public-institution requirements.
  • 18,374 villages were reported electrified under DDUGJY; the scheme closed on 31 March 2022.
  • Trap: Feeder separation is not the same benefit as an individual solar agricultural pump.

[Sources: Ministry of Power, 'Deen Dayal Upadhyaya Gram Jyoti Yojana', 27 November 2014, PIB; Ministry of Power, 'Implementation of Household Electrification under Saubhagya and RDSS', 23 December 2023, PIB Release 1989801; Ministry of Power, Lok Sabha Unstarred Question 2756, 'Definition of an Electrified Village', answered 2 August 2018; Ministry of Power, 'Electrification of Villages', 12 February 2026, PIB Release 2226925; consulted 16 November 2026.]

title: DDUGJY: Electrifying Villages and Strengthening Rural Networks

body:
From village electrification to household electrification

A village may have electricity-distribution lines without every household having an electricity connection. To address this remaining gap, the Government of India launched Pradhan Mantri Sahaj Bijli Har Ghar Yojana, commonly called Saubhagya, on 25 September 2017. It was a Ministry of Power scheme implemented with State Governments and distribution utilities.

Saubhagya's central objective was universal household electrification: providing electricity connections to willing households that did not already have them.

Which households were covered?

The scheme distinguished between rural and urban beneficiaries:

  • Rural areas: All willing unelectrified households were within its intended coverage.
  • Urban areas: The scheme specifically targeted willing unelectrified poor households.

Thus, the rural objective was wider than a programme restricted only to below-poverty-line households. It is equally important not to describe Saubhagya as offering connections to every non-poor urban household.

What did the connection benefit include?

The scheme supported last-mile connectivity from the distribution network to a household. The specified connection package included a service cable, an electricity meter, basic wiring for a light point with an LED bulb and a mobile-charging point. An additional electricity pole and associated conductor could be included where necessary.

Under the original scheme arrangements:

  • Eligible poor households received the electricity connection free of cost.
  • Other eligible households could receive a connection against ₹500, recoverable by the utility in 10 instalments through electricity bills.

Free connection does not mean free electricity consumption. Saubhagya did not provide a general entitlement to consume electricity without paying the applicable tariff. After connection, the household was responsible for its electricity charges under the relevant utility arrangements.

Achievements and closure

States reported the completion of electrification of identified willing households by 31 March 2019, with subsequent connections provided to additional eligible households identified later. The Ministry of Power reported that 2.86 crore households had been electrified during the Saubhagya period as of 31 March 2022.

Saubhagya closed on 31 March 2022. It should therefore be described as a completed historical scheme at the 16 November 2026 cutoff. Ongoing electrification needs are being addressed through other arrangements, including eligible works under RDSS; this does not mean that Saubhagya itself remains open.

Distinction from DDUGJY

DDUGJY primarily strengthened the rural electricity network and supported village electrification. Saubhagya concentrated on ensuring that individual willing households obtained connections, including in villages where electricity infrastructure already existed. The programmes were complementary, but their primary objectives were not identical.

Prelims focus

  • Full name: Pradhan Mantri Sahaj Bijli Har Ghar Yojana.
  • Launch: 25 September 2017; Ministry: Ministry of Power.
  • Coverage: willing unelectrified rural households and willing poor urban households.
  • Original connection charge: free for poor households; ₹500 in 10 instalments for other eligible households.
  • Reported achievement: 2.86 crore households during the scheme period; closure on 31 March 2022.
  • Trap: A free electricity connection is not a promise of free monthly electricity.

[Sources: Ministry of Power, 'FAQs on Pradhan Mantri Sahaj Bijli Har Ghar Yojana Saubhagya', 27 September 2017, especially Questions 1–4 and 6; Ministry of Power, 'Implementation of Household Electrification under Saubhagya and RDSS', 23 December 2023, PIB Release 1989801; Ministry of Power, 'Electrification of Villages', 12 February 2026, PIB Release 2226925; consulted 16 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: A 100-household village illustrates the historical 10% connection threshold, while Saubhagya targets all willing unelectrified rural households.
pictures.caption: Village electrification and household electrification are different measures.

title: Saubhagya: Electricity Connections to Unelectrified Households

body:
Objective, launch and authority

PM Surya Ghar: Muft Bijli Yojana is a Union programme for the installation of rooftop solar electricity systems in residential premises. It was launched on 13 February 2024 and approved by the Union Cabinet on 29 February 2024.

The nodal Union ministry is the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE). The scheme has an announced target of reaching 1 crore households.

Unlike a conventional household-electrification programme, PM Surya Ghar mainly helps an eligible electricity consumer become a small-scale producer of solar electricity by installing a rooftop photovoltaic system.

How rooftop solar serves a home

Solar photovoltaic panels convert sunlight into electrical energy. A rooftop system typically uses an inverter to provide electricity suitable for household appliances. Under an approved grid-connected arrangement, electricity generated by the rooftop system can serve the home, while the distribution grid supplies electricity when the solar system does not meet the household's requirements.

When generation exceeds immediate household use, surplus electricity may be exported to the distribution network under applicable State regulations. Billing and settlement depend on the approved metering arrangement and the consumer's electricity tariff.

Who can receive assistance?

The main central financial assistance is intended for eligible residential electricity consumers installing qualifying grid-connected rooftop solar systems. Implementation involves the National Portal, participating vendors and the relevant DISCOM, which performs required technical and metering functions.

Residential premises must meet the programme's applicable ownership, electricity-connection and technical conditions. A person does not become eligible merely because they are a farmer or own vacant land: those facts relate to different categories of solar programmes.

Central subsidy amounts

The Union Cabinet's approval of 29 February 2024 specified the following central financial assistance amounts at the prevailing benchmark rates:

Rooftop system capacityCentral subsidyImportant condition
1 kW₹30,000Eligible residential installation
2 kW₹60,000Eligible residential installation
3 kW₹78,000Central assistance reaches its capacity cap
Above 3 kW₹78,000No further increase in this standard central subsidy

The central assistance is capped at the equivalent of a 3 kW system. Any separate State incentive should not be confused with the amount of central assistance.

What does the reference to 300 units mean?

The scheme was announced with the objective of enabling households to obtain the benefit of up to 300 units of electricity per month through rooftop solar. This must not be interpreted as an unconditional entitlement under which every participating household receives 300 free units from its DISCOM irrespective of generation.

Actual solar generation depends on factors such as installed capacity, sunlight, system performance and the season. The resulting electricity bill depends on generation, household use and the applicable metering and tariff rules. A zero electricity bill is possible for some households under suitable conditions, but it is not guaranteed for every installation.

Status as of November 2026

PM Surya Ghar remained an active Union programme at the content cutoff. A Ministry of Information and Broadcasting backgrounder dated 13 November 2026 reported 65.26 lakh households benefiting as of 2 November 2026. This is a dated implementation figure, not the scheme's final target.

Prelims focus

  • Launch: 13 February 2024; Cabinet approval: 29 February 2024.
  • Ministry: MNRE; intended target: 1 crore households.
  • Beneficiaries: eligible residential consumers installing qualifying rooftop solar systems.
  • Standard central assistance: ₹30,000 for 1 kW; ₹60,000 for 2 kW; ₹78,000 for 3 kW or more.
  • Programme status on 16 November 2026: active.
  • Trap: The 300-unit objective is not an unconditional grant of 300 free grid units to every applicant.

[Sources: NCERT, India: People and Economy, Class 12, Chapter 7, 'Mineral and Energy Resources', section 'Non-Conventional Energy Sources'; MNRE, Cabinet approval of PM-Surya Ghar, PIB Release 2010133, 29 February 2024; MNRE, amendment to residential consumer assistance guidelines, Office Memorandum dated 7 July 2025; PIB, 'India's Renewable Energy Journey: Powering a Cleaner Future', 13 November 2026, Release 2335742, data as of 2 November 2026; consulted 16 November 2026.]
